chapter: Building the band, Ivie Anderson and touring
title: Wellman Braud, the string bass and Jean Goldkette's band
summary: Greer says the Kentucky Club had no bass, and Goldkette's band at Roseland amazed New York.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now did you -- when did Wellman Braud come in?

We never had a bass player at the Kentucky Club. The place was too small. He came in when we went to the Cotton Club, because it was only at that time the bass players were playing the tubas, but the first time we heard a string bass player was Steve, a white boy who came to New York with Jean Goldkette's band. We used to -- the Kentucky Club was just up the street, the next block, and we heard -- in fact, the whole New York aggregation, all the bands, none of them used string bass.

This guy Steve, I forget his last name, he came up with Jean Goldkette's band, up to the Roseland and was -- they were sensational! The news spread over New York, man, go up and hear Goldkette's band. New York had never heard of no band like Jean Goldkette's band out of Detroit and Steve was there, this boy from New Orleans, and he knew Braud -- at that time was just playing around New York, but he was playing a tuba and Braud told Duke, "Man, I'm going to get me a bass", that's how it all -- they were the only guys in New York, playing string bass.
This boy -- I never heard no cat play string bass and Braud he was something else, and he picked it up right away. This boy came with Jean Goldkette's band.
How did Jean Goldkette's band -- what
made it so different at that time?

I don't know, really, I don't know. It just sound different, that was it. Of course, Fletcher was the king up there, had Hawk and all them guys and Goldkette's talk... band washed them away. Man, that was the sensation of New York! Man go up with all the guys in Fletcher's band, "Man, you hear these guys? these guys are something else," and they started all that junk man, you know, then Fletcher got down to writing and carrying on, eventually come back, you know, on them. But Goldkette's band was something else.
Every musician in the world flocked to the Roseland to hear them cats play and they was something else.
Was it the writing or the soloists or both?

A combined organization. Not individuals, because individual, Fletcher was killing them, but they had all them arrangements and all that stuff, and they was something. They played together and they were really something.

Of course, Fletcher had Don Redman and all these -- Rex and all, all them guys up there and they would tear you up, we'd say dig, but this band come in as a collective group and when they had them tight arrangements, they was something else, man. You better believe it.
